headline: Washington drops its 13-year antitrust case; IBM shares jump 12%
text: On 8 January the Justice Department dropped the antitrust suit against IBM that it filed in 1969, which sought to break the company up. The government had spent 13.6 million dollars on it; Assistant Attorney General William Baxter said continuing would cost far more than the chance of winning was worth. Freed from the threat of being broken up, IBM shares rose 12% in January.
imageCaption: An IBM System/370 Model 168 mainframe installation

headline: An oil glut, and the oil-service darlings slide
text: The world has too much oil. Demand in the free world fell to about 47 million barrels a day in 1981 from 49.5 million in 1980, and in October OPEC cut its base price by 2 dollars to 34 dollars a barrel, the first cut since it was founded in 1960. Analysts are divided on whether the glut will last. Schlumberger's shares are down more than a third from their record of November 1980.
imageCaption: An offshore oil platform with its gas flare in the North Sea, 1975

headline: McDonald's keeps growing through the recession; McNuggets in test
text: McDonald's added 476 restaurants in 1981, bringing the total to 6,739, of which 5,554 are in the United States and 1,185 in 29 other countries and territories; it opened its first restaurants in Spain, Denmark and the Philippines. Its record growth continued despite the recession. Chicken McNuggets, bite-sized fried chicken created by its first executive chef René Arend, were introduced in selected markets in 1981.

headline: Gold falls to 330 dollars as inflation retreats
text: Gold averaged 330 dollars in March, 12 percent below February, the lowest since August 1979 and less than half its January 1980 average. Inflation has dropped to 7.6 percent (February) while the rate banks charge each other is near 15 percent, so money in the bank earns about 7 percent more than prices rise. The prime rate stands at 16.5 percent.
imageCaption: A vault stacked with gold bars

headline: The three big Swiss banks are now available to you
text: From this month you can buy shares of Switzerland's three big banks. The Schweizerische Bankgesellschaft of Zurich is the largest: it manages the wealth of private clients from all over the world, lends to Swiss companies and households, and trades securities. The Schweizerischer Bankverein of Basel is strong in the international securities and currency markets. The Schweizerische Kreditanstalt of Zurich, called Credit Suisse abroad, is still recovering its reputation from the Chiasso scandal of 1977, in which a branch near the Italian border ran a fraudulent scheme that cost the bank about 1.4 billion francs; since 1978 it has been partnered with the US investment bank First Boston.

headline: Goizueta's two bets: Columbia Pictures and Diet Coke
text: Coca-Cola unveiled Diet Coke on 8 July and launched it in New York City; it is to reach most of the United States by the end of the year. It is the first new product to carry the Coca-Cola trademark since 1886. Last month the company agreed to buy the Hollywood studio Columbia Pictures for about 750 million dollars, a controversial move: chairman Goizueta argues entertainment has good growth prospects and can use Coca-Cola's skill in market research. Pepsi has been gaining market share in soft drinks.
imageCaption: The Rockettes at the 'world premiere' of Diet Coke, Radio City Music Hall, New York, July 1982

headline: Wall Street jumps on rate hopes; Boeing up 48%, Apple up 33%
text: After the Dow hit a low of 777 on 12 August, it jumped a record 39 points on the 17th, when an influential Salomon Brothers economist said interest rates would fall, and trading topped 100 million shares a day for the first time. The shares that had fallen furthest rose most: Boeing gained 48% in August and Apple Computer 33%. On 19 August Boeing delivered its first 767 to United Airlines.

headline: Gold jumps 20 percent as rates fall and Mexico wobbles
text: Gold averaged 437 dollars in September, 20 percent more than in August and almost 40 percent above its June average. Falling interest rates make gold cheaper to hold, and Mexico's announcement in August that it cannot pay its foreign debts has raised fears for the banks that lent to it. Ten-year Treasury yields averaged 12.3 percent, down from 14.3 percent in June.
imageCaption: President Reagan hosts Mexico's President Jose Lopez Portillo at Camp David
imageCredit: White House Photographic Office, Reagan Library

headline: Falling interest rates power a second leap
text: By October inflation had fallen to about 5% and long-term interest rates were coming down as the Federal Reserve let its key rate fall back to about 9%. The stock market rose another 11% in October. Apple, the best-known maker of personal computers, is one of the most popular growth stocks.
imageCaption: Paul Volcker, chairman of the Federal Reserve, with President Reagan at the White House
imageCredit: President (1981-1989 : Reagan). White House Photographic Off

headline: Retail stocks lead the new bull market
text: Since the Federal Reserve cut its discount rate in mid-August, share prices have surged, with record trading of 149 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange on 4 November. Shares of retailers that sell to consumers are among the biggest winners as investors bet on falling interest rates and a recovery in spending.

headline: BMW launches the new 3 Series
text: BMW released the second generation of its compact 3 Series at the end of November. For the first time it will also come as a four-door saloon, so that it suits families, not only enthusiasts.
imageCaption: A first-generation BMW 3 Series (E21) on the road

headline: 1982 in review: from the August low to records
text: The S&P 500 rose 15% in 1982 to 140.64, and the Dow gained 19.6% to 1,046.54, its best year in seven, after reaching an all-time high of 1,070.55 on 27 December. From the August low the Dow is up 37.7%. A record 16.46 billion shares traded on the New York Stock Exchange, while unemployment is near 11 percent, the highest since the war.

headline: IBM buys 12% of Intel for 250 million dollars
text: IBM agreed on 22 December to buy 12% of Intel's shares for 250 million dollars, at 40 dollars a share, with the option to go up to 30%. Intel makes the chips in IBM's personal computers, and the cash helps it through the recession.
imageCaption: "Keeping up with modern times": IBM's advertisement for its Personal Computer, which runs on Intel's 8088 chip, with the Charlie Chaplin tramp, 1982
imageCredit: IBM advertisement, from Personal Computing, May 1982 (scan: nosher.net)

headline: Mercedes launches the 190, its first compact car
text: Daimler-Benz has put the Mercedes 190 and 190 E on the market, the first compact car of the brand. Daimler has spent eight years and a fortune developing it, with advanced suspension and lightweight high-strength steel.
